title: To whom shall we go? (John 6:52–71)
hook: many leave; Peter says: you have the words of eternal life

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crowd asked for manna, and Jesus said: I am the bread of life. Your line was bread of life. Did you pause before a meal? Day six hundred eleven.

There's a moment in a lot of friendships, and a lot of faiths, when the thing gets hard. The easy early days are over. Something is said that you can't quite follow, or can't quite accept. And you look around, and other people are quietly leaving. This is that moment in John's Gospel. Jesus has been teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum about bread from heaven, and the teaching gets stranger and stronger. Even his own followers start muttering among themselves. In the King James Bible they say: "This is an hard saying; who can hear it?"

What was so hard? Jesus had said that unless they eat his flesh and drink his blood, they have no life in them. His hearers take it as literally as anyone would, and they recoil. Christians have understood these words in different ways ever since. Catholic and Orthodox Christians hear in them the Eucharist, the bread and wine that become, in their teaching, the body and blood of Christ. Lutherans speak of Christ truly present in the bread and wine. Many other Protestants understand the words as a picture of faith: taking Christ in, the way bread is taken into the body. All of them agree the words are meant to be taken with complete seriousness. And in the story, the result is the same. "From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him." Not enemies. Disciples. People who had followed him. So Jesus turns to the twelve and asks the hardest question of all: "Will ye also go away?" He doesn't beg them to stay. He doesn't soften what he said. He just asks. And Peter, who so often says the wrong thing, says exactly the right one: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." Listen to how honest that is. Peter doesn't say, I understand everything you just said. He doesn't say, it was easy to hear. He says, where else would we go? Sometimes faith isn't certainty. It's knowing you've found where life is, even on the days you don't understand it. Peter speaks for the twelve. But John adds a sad note: Jesus already knows one of the twelve will betray him.
screen: then, large: `LORD, TO WHOM SHALL WE GO?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay with what gives you life. Settle, and breathe. Think of something that gives you life but has gotten hard lately. A friendship. A marriage. A practice like this one. A faith, if you have one. Notice the part of you that's tempted to walk away quietly. Don't scold it. Then ask Peter's question honestly: if I leave, where would I go? What would I lose? If you pray, you can tell God plainly what's hard. If you don't, simply hold the thing that gives you life, and choose it for today. The bell holds the time.
To whom shall we go? Peter's answer when many disciples left: thou hast the words of eternal life.

segments.voice: Your line: to whom else? Today, stay one minute longer with something hard that you know gives you life. Day six hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Christians often turn to Peter's words in seasons of doubt; in some churches, his line is sung or said before the Gospel is read.

original.note: Greek: words, sayings. "Thou hast the words of eternal life."

trapdoor: what you thought: Peter making a confident statement of faith.
what it means: in a moment when many walk away, Peter admits there's nowhere else to go, because this is where life is.
what a scholar hears: John's version of Peter's confession, parallel to Caesarea Philippi in the other Gospels, set right after a teaching churches read in different ways.

notes: Church positions on 6:53–58: Catholic and Orthodox (Eucharistic real presence/transformation), Lutheran (real presence), many other Protestants (faith reading; some Reformed speak of spiritual presence). Confirm fair summary.
'His line is sung or said before the Gospel is read' (howItsDone): some liturgies use John 6:68 as a Gospel acclamation verse; confirm or soften.
John 6:59 places the teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum. Confirm.
Trapdoor parallels Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi (Matthew 16, Mark 8); confirm.
